title: Piano and Guitar Together
intro: Piano and guitar cover the same range and both play chords, so played together without a plan they blur into each other. Arranging for both means giving each its own register, rhythm and role.

items: One instrument keeps the rhythm, the other sustains: guitar strums eighths while the piano holds whole-note chords, or the piano plays a pulsing pattern while the guitar picks single notes.
One takes the low end, one the middle: if the piano plays bass notes, the guitar avoids string 6 and plays triads on the top strings (see Chord Voicings (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/chord-voicings)).
Trade roles between sections: guitar leads the verse, piano the chorus.

blocks.text: A strummed open-position guitar chord covers roughly E2 to E4, exactly where a piano player's hands like to sit. Move one of them: piano voicings an octave higher (around C4–C6) over a strummed guitar, or the guitar up the neck with a capo or small triads over a full piano. The low register needs the most care: two instruments playing different bass notes, or bass notes with thirds, turn to mud below about C3 (see Consonance and Dissonance (#/arts/music-theory/intervals/consonance)).

widget.title: Muddy versus clear: the same C chord shared by two instruments

examples.label: Clash: guitar C shape plus a piano chord with thirds low in the bass
Clear: guitar shape low, piano voiced high

blocks.text: Agree on the chords and voicings

Both players must use the same chord, but not the same voicing. Extensions can clash: if the piano plays Cmaj7 (with B) while the guitar strums C with a C on top, the B and C rub a semitone apart. Agree on the colour notes (7ths, 9ths, sus) per chord, or let one instrument play simple triads while the other adds colour. Slash chords matter too: if the piano plays C/E with E in the bass, the guitar should not hammer the C on string 5, fret 3, of the open C shape.

Guitarists like sharp keys (E, A, D, G); pianists are equally at home in flat keys. For keys like E♭ or A♭, the guitarist can use a capo (G shapes at fret 1 sound A♭, C shapes at fret 3 sound E♭) so both play comfortably. Two guitarists, or a guitarist and the piano's right hand, can also use different shape families for the same chords to fill the space (one in open C shapes, one with a capo at 5 in G shapes).

Give each instrument a different rhythmic layer: piano on downbeats and the guitar on the offbeats ('skank' in reggae), or the guitar on a steady eighth-note strum while the piano answers the vocal phrases with short fills. When both play the same rhythm, align their accents exactly; a near-miss sounds sloppy.

blocks.title: Arrange it
blocks.text: A song is in E♭ major and the guitarist only knows open shapes. Where should the capo go if they use C shapes, and what should the pianist avoid?
solution: From C to E♭ is 3 semitones: capo at fret 3 with C shapes (C, F, G, Am shapes sound E♭, A♭, B♭, Cm). The capoed guitar sits roughly G2–G4. The pianist should voice right-hand chords higher (around E♭5 and up, or E♭4–E♭5 only if the guitar stays low), keep the left hand to roots and octaves, and avoid doubling the guitar's middle register.
blocks.answer: Capo 3 with C shapes; the piano voices higher and keeps the low end simple

blocks.text: Sources: Blatter, A. (1997). Instrumentation and Orchestration, 2nd ed. Schirmer; Perricone, J. (2018). Great Songwriting Techniques. Oxford University Press; Pejrolo, A. & DeRosa, R. (2016). Acoustic and MIDI Orchestration for the Contemporary Composer, 2nd ed. Focal Press.
